item.title: Panthers' JJ Jansen to play his 282nd game, most ever for a long snapper
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Carolina's JJ Jansen will become the NFL's all-time record holder for games played by a long snapper on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Carolina's JJ Jansen will become the NFL's all-time record holder for games played by a long snapper on Sunday.

The Panthers-Eagles game will be Jansen's 282nd, breaking a tie with Trey Junkin for the most games played at long snapper in NFL history.

The 40-year-old Jansen long snapped at Notre Dame and then signed with the Packers as an undrafted free agent in 2008 but played only in the preseason, spending the regular season on injured reserve. In 2009 the Panthers needed a long snapper, so they traded a conditional 2011 draft pick for Jansen. He's been their long snapper ever since.

Long snapping is a skill that few players ever learn, and most who do have a story of a football mentor who taught them the technique that can earn playing time on the varsity high school team, a college scholarship for some, and NFL riches for a select few. For Jansen, that mentor was his father, who had been a high school long snapper.

"I still remember we practiced in the same way every single time," Jansen told Darin Gantt of Panthers.com. "We had like a square piece of grass that was probably 20 yards by 20 yards. I'd stand at one end in front of a tree that was right in the middle. My dad would stand at 15 yards away, and I would snap it. We'd have those legendary long nights where you're good, and then you stink, and then you're good, and you stink, and you're mad at yourself because you stink, so you yell at your dad, and he's yelling back at you and, there's this whole, you know, boys and their fathers moments."

Jansen has played the second-most games of any active player, behind only Ravens defensive end Calais Campbell, who has played 283 games. If both Campbell and Jansen play all 17 games this season, at the end of the year Campbell will have played 295 games, tying him with Darrell Green for the 16th-most in NFL history, and Jansen will have played 294, good for 18th-most in NFL history.

All 281 of Jansen's games have been with the Panthers. Former Lions kicker Jason Hanson has the NFL record for most games played with one team, at 327. If Jansen keeps playing every game in Carolina, he'll move ahead of Hanson in the final game of the 2028 season. Jansen is showing no signs of slowing down.

item.title: Chiefs nose tackle Khyiris Tonga is playing almost as much offense as Travis Hunter
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Jaguars cornerback/wide receiver Travis Hunter has been much-hyped for his status as a two-way player, first as a Heisman Trophy winner at Colorado and now in the NFL.
item.content:encoded:
Jaguars cornerback/wide receiver Travis Hunter has been much-hyped for his status as a two-way player, first as a Heisman Trophy winner at Colorado and now in the NFL. But there's another two-way player in the NFL this season who hasn't received as much hype: Chiefs nose tackle and fullback Khyiris Tonga.

Like Hunter, Tonga has started every game on defense this season. Like Hunter, Tonga has played only limited offensive snaps this season. Tonga has two carries; Hunter has two catches. Both have picked up one first down.

Hunter plays a little bit more on offense, but not much more: Hunter has played 6.8 percent of the Jaguars' offensive snaps, while Tonga has played 4.2 percent of the Chiefs' offensive snaps.

The Jaguars have said Hunter is capable of being a full-time player at both wide receiver and cornerback, while the Chiefs consider Tonga only a situational short-yardage fullback in addition to his duties as a starter on the defensive line. But as far as their usage this season, both players are comparable.

Patriots coach Mike Vrabel, himself a former defensive player who occasionally lined up on offense as well, started using Tonga as a blocking fullback last season, when Tonga played 14 snaps on offense in New England. This year, Tonga signed a three-year, $21 million free agent contract with the Chiefs, and the Chiefs have increased his role on offense, including not just blocking but also running the ball.

Tonga said on the Chiefs’ YouTube channel that it was a thrill the first time he went into the offensive huddle with quarterback Patrick Mahomes and running back Kenneth Walker.

"It was super cool," Tonga said. "Being in the offensive huddle is amazing, especially having the players we have, to share the huddle with them. The only thing in my mind was, Don't mess it up. I just went out there to have fun. It makes it easy blocking for a guy like K9."

Tonga even ran a route on a fourth-and-goal touchdown pass to Jalen Royals in Week 2, and Tonga said he was prepared to catch it if Mahomes threw to him but was a little relieved when Mahomes looked past him and threw to Royals.

"I was just making sure I didn't drop it. Look it in if it came to me. It went past me, so it was OK," Tonga said.

Could Tonga do anything else in Andy Reid's offense? He said he'd even be up for throwing the ball on a trick play if that gets called.

"Having a guy like 15, I hope they don't make me throw the ball, but if we have to I'm ready," Tonga said.

Tonga, who has also played 19 snaps on special teams this season, is willing to do whatever he has to do to help his team win.

item.title: Titans CEO Burke Nihill: Our organization believes in coach Robert Saleh, GM Mike Borgonzi
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Titans have fired a head coach or GM each of the last four years, but they say they're going to be patient with their current coach and GM.
item.content:encoded:
The Titans are 0-5 in head coach Robert Saleh's first season, and 3-19 five games into General Manager Mike Borgonzi's second season. But Titans CEO Burke Nihill says the franchise believes the right leadership is in place.

"I personally feel a sense of stability," Nihill told ESPN on Friday. "I believe that Mike Borgonzi and Robert Saleh are ultimately going to get this team out of the woods and restore it to competitive football. The train is on the tracks. It just hasn't picked up momentum, but it will. I can confidently say this organization is in a place where there is organizational belief in Mike, in Robert, and they absolutely have all the support they need to get this train moving and moving faster."

Those comments would mean more coming directly from Titans owner Amy Adams-Strunk, but the ESPN report says Nihill is empowered to speak for her. Nihill says the organization knows the fans are frustrated.

"The first thing I would say back to the fans is just that we're sorry," Nihill said. "There's nobody in this building that doesn't feel . . . a sense of grief about it, because not only are we fans of the team as well, but we feel the sense of responsibility to deliver. And we've let our fans down because football is supposed to be fun. I think it starts on the field and the state of the franchise. We're 0-5, and that's not nearly good enough. It hasn't been for a while."

The Titans fired General Manager Jon Robinson during the 2022 season, fired head coach Mike Vrabel after the 2023 season, fired General Manager Ran Carthon after the 2024 season and fired head coach Brian Callahan during the 2025 season. All those firings haven't turned the franchise around. Now they're pledging patience with Borgonzi and Saleh.

item.title: 19.8 million watched Bills-Rams on Monday night
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Monday night instant classic between the Bills and the Rams nevertheless failed to crack the 20 million viewer threshold on the various Disney networks.
item.content:encoded:
The Monday night instant classic between the Bills and the Rams nevertheless failed to crack the 20 million viewer threshold on the various Disney networks.

Via ESPN, the final game of Week 5, broadcast by ABC, ESPN, ESPN2, ESPN Deportes, and NFL Network, generated 19.8 million viewers.

It's the second most-watched Week 5 Monday night game since ESPN assumed the package in 2026; last year's Chiefs-Jaguars game holds the Week 5 record.

ESPN also announced that the alternate broadcasts on ESPN2 (the ManningCast) and NFL Network (a NextGen Stats production) attracted 1.1 million viewers, without specifying the audiences on either network.

That approach could be a precursor to the upcoming Pat McAfee alt casts on ESPN2; if ESPN2 and NFL Network audiences are lumped together, there won't be a clear, apples-to-apples comparison between the ManningCast and the McAfeeFest.

In the end, none of the Week 5 prime-time games surpassed 20 million. Bills-Rams arguably was the best candidate to get there, given the Super Bowl preview sizzle associated with the game, and the involvement of the last two NFL MVPs (Bills quarterback Josh Allen and Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford).

item.title: Troy Aikman's role with the Dolphins hovers over his broadcasting future
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Why would any network with options opt for someone who works for one of the NFL's teams?
item.content:encoded:
Troy Aikman's contract with ESPN expires after the 2026 season, which culminates in the four-letter network's first ever Super Bowl. Absent an extension, which Aikman currently doesn't expect, he'll become a broadcasting free agent.

His separate relationship with the Dolphins hovers over Aikman's future on TV.

Via Mark Maske of Front Office Sports, Aikman does not have a “formal and ongoing agreement” to serve as a consultant with the Dolphins. This means that he's working for the team on an at-will basis, and that he (or the team) can end the relationship at any time.

It could be in Aikman's best interests to end the relationship with the Dolphins now. If ESPN (or CBS or Prime Video) will be paying $20 million or more for its top NFL analyst gig, why would any of them hire someone who has both restrictions on his access and a cloud over his objectivity, thanks to having an employment relationship with one of its teams.

Last month, Aikman "called bullshit" on the idea that other broadcasters don't have conflicts of interest. That misses the point. Aikman is employed by the Dolphins. That relationship prevents him from entering team facilities or attending practices — and it creates avoidable complications when it comes to games involving the team that employs him.

When ESPN's Jason Kelce refers to the Eagles as "we," it's because he used to play for the team. (And ESPN is trying to get him to knock it off.) When Aikman talks about the Dolphins, "we" is technically accurate; he works for the team.

For networks with options, why would any network opt for someone who is employed by one of the teams? Beyond Tom Brady (who owns a piece of the Raiders and has an even more obvious conflict of interest, even if Fox doesn't care), none of the other candidates for the biggest jobs in NFL broadcasting bring such baggage with them.

As to Aikman, the right decision is obvious if he hopes to get another high-profile broadcasting job. He should end his relationship with the Dolphins as soon as possible.

item.title: Terrion Arnold remains on paid leave
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The NFL's decision to reinstate Packers running back Josh Jacobs and Broncos linebacker Jonathon Cooper from the Commissioner Exempt list carried with it a conspicuous omission.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL's decision to reinstate Packers running back Josh Jacobs and Broncos linebacker Jonathon Cooper from the Commissioner Exempt list carried with it a conspicuous omission.

Seahawks cornerback Terrion Arnold remains on paid leave.

All three landed on paid leave on Sunday, August 30. Both Jacobs and Cooper are returning after six games. Arnold will continue to wait.

The distinction highlights the evolution of paid leave. Now, the NFL uses it as a way to pre-suspend a player with pay for the number of games he's likely to miss once officially suspended under the Personal Conduct Policy. The player receives credit once he's suspended without pay for the games missed while on paid leave.

As to Arnold, who faces a potential sentence of life in prison due to eight felonies arising from an alleged armed robbery and kidnapping, it makes sense for the league to wait for the criminal case against him to be resolved. While the standard punishment for a case of domestic battery is six games, the claims against Arnold could trigger something longer — especially in light of the potential criminal penalties.

Frankly, the NFL may never have to convert Arnold's paid leave into an unpaid suspension. If he ends up behind bars for the practical balance of his career, the length of the suspension won't matter.

item.description: The Lions took care of some roster business during their bye week.
item.content:encoded:
The Lions took care of some roster business during their bye week.

They announced that they have placed offensive lineman Ben Bartch, wide receiver Tom Kennedy, and linebacker Devin White on the injured reserve list. All three players will have to miss at least four games before they'll have a chance to return.

Bartch was inactive in Week 5 due to a foot injury and White broke his forearm in that game. Kennedy is expected to miss the rest of the season with an MCL injury that requires surgery.

The Lions now have three open roster spots to fill. Safety Brian Branch and center Cade Mays have designated for return from injured reserve, so they could take two of those slots.

item.title: KC Concepcion on Minkah Fitzpatrick's hit: It was a football play; it wasn't dirty
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Jets safety Minkah Fitzpatrick's hit on KC Concepcion on Sunday knocked out the Browns wide receiver.
item.content:encoded:
Jets safety Minkah Fitzpatrick's hit on KC Concepcion on Sunday knocked out the Browns wide receiver. Concepcion was diagnosed with his first concussion.

Fitzpatrick will appeal a fine from the NFL, calling the hit just a "football play" despite a 15-yard unnecessary roughness penalty.

Concepcion agrees with Fitzpatrick's assessment.

“I know the game that I signed up to play,” Concepcion said Friday, via Mary Kay Cabot of cleveland.com. “This game is a very physical game. To me, it wasn’t a dirty hit. It was just a football play.”

The rookie first-round pick cleared concussion protocol on Friday and will play Sunday.

“I thank the Lord, just for him allowing me to get back up and be able to walk off the field,” Concepcion said. “I’m like this all the time, smiling, dancing, cracking jokes. [But] I would say that I am glad that I was able to get up and be able to play again.”

item.title: Stephen Jones says Joey Porter Jr. is "all-in" with the Cowboys
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Cowboys cornerback Joey Porter Jr. did not play in four games with the Steelers.
item.content:encoded:
Cowboys cornerback Joey Porter Jr. did not play in four games with the Steelers. He was inactive due to his on-again, off-again back issue, which wasn't an issue after the trade to the Cowboys.

Porter, though, has had an ankle injury and an illness, playing one of two possible games in Dallas.

He is questionable for Sunday's game against the Packers.

Porter was unhappy with the Steelers after not getting a desired long-term contract extension before the season. The Cowboys made clear after the trade that they aren't negotiating with Porter this season.

Cowboys executive vice president Stephen Jones was asked on 105.3 The Fan whether he had concerns about a hold-in from Porter.

“Oh, absolutely, I think he’s all in," Jones said on his radio show Friday, via Jon Machota of TheAthletic.com. "He wants to be out there. He was sick [in Week 5 against the Bucs]. He couldn’t play last week with the flu. But he obviously played in our [Week 4 game against the Texans], and I think he’s fired up about what he can do to help us win against the Packers.”

Porter said earlier this week that he expects to have a full-time role in the defense against the Packers.

item.title: John Lynch: George Kittle asked me if we're trying to trade for Khalil Mack
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The trade deadline was a topic of conversation for General Manager John Lynch on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
The trade deadline was a topic of conversation for General Manager John Lynch on Friday.

Lynch was a guest on KNBR and he was asked if calls are picking up with the November 10 deadline drawing closer. Lynch said that the calls have picked up of late and that the team has made its own "just to kind of see where the market's at" right now.

Lynch was also asked specifically about interest in Chargers pass rusher Khalil Mack.

"I can’t tell you that," Lynch said, via 49ersWebzone.com. "A lot of people ask me that. We seem to be connected to everyone, and I don't know where that comes from. I had a player ask me that yesterday."

Lynch eventually named tight end George Kittle as the inquisitive player, which isn't surprising "because he asks about everything." Kittle's interest in the prospect makes sense, however. The 49ers are 5-0 and should feel good enough about their chances to make a run that they'd be willing to bolster the roster ahead of the deadline. On the other hand, the Chargers are 0-5 and should be considering picking up assets for the future with this season headed off the rails.

item.description: The Eagles will have their top receiver back for Sunday, but they won't have another one of their top offensive players.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles will have their top receiver back for Sunday, but they won't have another one of their top offensive players.

While DeVonta Smith (hamstring/toe) will play in the Week 6 matchup against the Panthers, running back Saquon Barkley (hamstring) has been ruled out.

Smith was a full participant in Friday's practice. He told reporters that he was feeling good, but he’d leave the decision as to whether or not he’d play up to the doctors.

They’ve apparently given Smith the OK after he missed the last two games.

Smith has 19 catches for 235 yards with one touchdown so far in 2026.

Barkley did not practice all week.

Defensive back Michael Carter (abdomen), outside linebacker Jalyx Hunt (knee/ankle), running back Will Shipley (foot), and quarterback Jalen Hurts (calf) have been ruled out. Shipley has been placed on injured reserve, the team announced.

Outside linebacker A.J. Epenesa (back) is doubtful.

Cornerback Jakorian Bennett (knee), tight end Grant Calcaterra (back), guard Landon Dickerson (knee), offensive lineman Drew Kendall (knee), and tight end Eli Stowers (quad) are all questionable.

Linebacker Zack Baun (shoulder), receiver Marquise Brown (ankle), linebacker Jihaad Campbell (knee/wrist), defensive tackle Jalen Carter (wrist), outside linebacker Arnold Ebiketie (shoulder), safety Marcus Epps (groin), outside linebacker Jonathan Greenard (ankle), tight end E.J. item.title: NFL removes Broncos OLB Jonathon Cooper from Commissioner's Exempt List
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The NFL has announced it has removed Broncos outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper from the Commissioner's Exempt List.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL has announced it has removed Broncos outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper from the Commissioner's Exempt List.

Cooper is eligible to play in the team's next game on Oct. 25 after missing six games.

The NFL placed Cooper on paid leave on Aug. 30 following domestic-related charges involving two incidents with his former girlfriend in June.

Cooper's motion hearing was continued on Monday at the request of the district attorney’s office. He is now scheduled for a motion hearing on Feb. 23 and a jury trial the week of March 2. The NFL season ends with Super Bowl LXI on Feb. 14.

Cooper is facing five charges after two disputes with his ex-girlfriend that began with a fight over a cell phone. The most serious charge is felony second-degree assault/strangulation.

He participated in the team's training camp and three preseason games after pleading not guilty to all charges.

Cooper lost $180,000 in per-game roster bonuses but was able to keep his six weekly game checks of $676,471 each while on leave.

In its statement, the league said it will continue to investigate and monitor Cooper's legal matter until a resolution.

item.title: Josh Jacobs will be removed from paid leave on Monday
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: NFL leaves door open for further discipline.
item.content:encoded:
The efforts of Packers running back Josh Jacobs to keep the NFL from seeing the video of the altercation that resulted in his no-contest plea for battery has worked. For now.

The NFL has announced that Jacobs will be reinstated from the Commissioner Exempt list on Monday.

The timing isn't coincidental. With the baseline punishment for domestic battery under the Personal Conduct Policy set at six games, the move allows the league to pre-suspend a player whose internal investigation is still pending. Then, if/when a suspension is imposed, he'll get credit for the games missed while on paid leave — and he'll forfeit the pay he received during the games in which he didn't play.

Although paid leave technically isn't discipline (even though, as a practical matter, it is), the missed games become part of the eventual discipline. And the league's decision to reserve the right to add additional games ties directly to the video that it wants to review before it closes his case.

It's a risky move for the NFL. Until it sees the video, it won't know whether the video contains images that would justify a much more significant punishment than a six-game suspension. The better play, given Jacobs's efforts to keep the league from seeing the video, would be to tell him that he won't play at all until the league sees the video.

If, in the end, the video is as shocking as the Ray Rice video from 2014 was, the NFL will have another P.R. mess on its hands. Maybe, after 12 years, the memory of extent of the Ray Rice situation has faded. Either way, the safest approach would have been to tell Jacobs that, until the video is seen by the league, his stay on paid leave will continue.

item.title: David Blough takes responsibility for clock debacle
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: When a soldier is captured by the enemy, he knows to say only three things: Name, rank, and serial number.
item.content:encoded:
When a soldier is captured by the enemy, he knows to say only three things: Name, rank, and serial number. As to the Commanders' overtime clock debacle against the Giants, a similar three-step formula has emerged.

It's my responsibility. I take accountability. It won't happen again.

Offensive coordinator David Blough completed the fault trifecta on Friday, in his first comments to reporters since the Week 5 game ended in a tie, thanks to a stunning failure to find a way to attempt a field goal in the final 55 seconds of the extra 10-minute period, Blough repeatedly expressed a very basic, general message of responsibility, acceptance of accountability, and determination to not let the situation repeat itself.

The reporters tried to get more (any) details from him about how it transpired. He continued to retreat to a combination of words and phrases that eventually seemed to be the product of talking points that had been prepared and memorized at some point this week.

Ultimately, there has been no real insight from coach Dan Quinn, quarterback Jayden Daniels, or Blough into how it happened. And none of them has been asked the one question that may have yielded the most revealing answer: Did the quarterback and the rest of the offense realize that the game would end when the 10 minutes expired?

At this point, with a new slate of Sunday games looming (and with the Commanders facing the 49ers on Monday night), the incident will become a footnote to the 2026 season. And we'll never know precisely how it happened.

We know what happened — they screwed up, royally. But we'll never know how it happened, why it happened, and, ultimately, who bears the bulk of the blame.

Yes, it's everyone. Still, there's someone who deserves more blame than others. And there's a specific explanation (beyond "shit happens") as to how it came to be. That explanation, through multiple press availabilities, never emerged.

item.title: After Gayle Benson attends Saints practice, Kellen Moore says they're "all good"
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Saints owner Gayle Benson attended practice today and hugged coach Kellen Moore, says after she said she won't accept the way the team is playing.
item.content:encoded:
Saints owner Gayle Benson attended practice today and hugged coach Kellen Moore, says after she said she won’t accept the way the team is playing. Moore said he and Benson are on the same page.

"It's always good to see Mrs. B," Moore said after practice. "She likes to pop in and catch practice here and there, so always good to see her. She's always looking great and always supportive."

Moore tried to cool down any talk that he and his boss are not on the same page, given Benson's comments about the 1-4 Saints.

"We see each other throughout these seasons and it was great," Benson said.

Moore said he has talked to Benson since she made her public comments about the team's performance being unacceptable and he feels confident in the direction they're going.

"We talked throughout the week and so we're all good," Moore said. "We're all just trying to reach the same goal. We all want to win football games and so we're all working toward that. I think this was a good week for our guys, coaches, players. A really good week of practice."

Soon, Moore is going to need to show that his team can translate good practices into good games, or else Benson will be more likely to give him a pink slip than a hug.
